raw_case_text:
An 11-year-old female patient from Kenya presented to the urology clinic with a six-month history of recurrent painless gross hematuria without clots, associated with storage symptoms including urinary frequency and occasional urgency. She had no relevant medical or surgical history and was otherwise healthy. Although she was born and residing in the UAE, her family reported occasional short visits to Kenya (approximately once every one to two years for brief stays), indicating limited but notable exposure risk in an endemic environment. 
Physical examination revealed a hemodynamically stable, afebrile child with a soft, non-tender abdomen and no palpable masses. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, renal profile, and electrolytes, were within normal limits, with no eosinophilia or anemia. Urinalysis demonstrated numerous red blood cells and elevated white blood cells, while urine culture demonstrated no bacterial growth, indicating sterile pyuria (Table 1).
Urine cytology was performed early due to persistent painless hematuria despite negative cultures, to evaluate for rare etiologies such as parasitic ova or malignant cells. Cytology revealed Schistosoma haematobium eggs in a hemorrhagic and suppurative background with no malignant features. 
Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) revealed floating intraluminal echoes within the urinary bladder (Figure 1).
CT urography demonstrated thin, patchy calcifications along the inner bladder wall consistent with submucosal calcifications (Figure 2).
Cystourethroscopy was performed under general anesthesia and revealed extensive sandy patches covering the bladder mucosa. Cold-cup biopsies were obtained from both lateral bladder walls, the posterior bladder wall, and the trigone (Figure 3).
Histopathology demonstrated preserved urothelial morphology with Schistosoma haematobium ova associated with a giant-cell reaction, with no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy. 
The patient was treated with praziquantel at a single oral dose of 40 mg/kg, repeated after four weeks. Treatment was well-tolerated without adverse effects. At six-month follow-up, she was asymptomatic, and repeat urinalysis and urine cytology showed no Schistosoma haematobium ova. Ultrasound KUB was normal, and renal function remained stable (Table 2).
The family received education about schistosomiasis transmission and prevention. She was placed on long-term surveillance with periodic urinalysis and imaging due to the risk of delayed complications in chronic schistosomiasis.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old girl presented with a 6-month history of recurrent painless gross hematuria without clots accompanied by urinary frequency and occasional urgency.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 6 months, the child experienced recurrent episodes of painless, clot-free gross hematuria associated with urinary storage symptoms including frequency and occasional urgency.
subjective.past_medical_history: Otherwise healthy with no prior medical or surgical history. Born and residing in the United Arab Emirates, with periodic short family visits to Kenya (approximately once every 1-2 years).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for urinary frequency and occasional urgency; no other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable and afebrile with a soft, non-tender abdomen and no palpable masses.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, renal profile, and serum electrolytes were normal without eosinophilia or anemia. Urinalysis showed numerous RBCs and elevated WBCs, while urine culture showed no bacterial growth (sterile pyuria). Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) revealed floating intraluminal echoes within the urinary bladder.
objective.advanced_workup: Urine cytology demonstrated Schistosoma haematobium eggs in a hemorrhagic, suppurative background without malignant cells. CT urography revealed thin, patchy submucosal calcifications along the inner bladder wall. Cystourethroscopy under general anesthesia showed extensive sandy patches across the bladder mucosa, and cold-cup biopsies from the bilateral lateral walls, posterior wall, and trigone demonstrated preserved urothelium with Schistosoma haematobium ova surrounded by a giant-cell reaction without dysplasia or malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed urinary schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium based on urine cytology, CT urography, cystoscopy, and bladder biopsy histopathology. She was treated with a single oral dose of praziquantel 40 mg/kg repeated after 4 weeks, which was well tolerated. At 6-month follow-up, she was completely asymptomatic with normal KUB ultrasound, stable renal function, and negative repeat urinalysis and urine cytology for S. haematobium ova.
